◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Magnetism and electricity are two faces of one force. Moving charges create magnetic fields, and magnetic fields push moving charges — the principle behind every electric motor, generator, speaker, and hard drive. It is also the gateway to understanding light itself.

Magnetism arises from moving charges. A magnetic field exerts a force on charges that move through it (and on current-carrying wires), and electric currents in turn create magnetic fields — the deep link called electromagnetism.

Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge

Force on a moving charge
A charge q moving at speed v through a magnetic field B feels a force F = qvB (when v is perpendicular to B). The force is perpendicular to both v and B, and a stationary charge feels no magnetic force.
Force on a current-carrying wire
A wire of length L carrying current I in a field B feels a force F = BIL (for perpendicular orientation). This is what makes motors turn.
🧠 ANALOGY

The magnetic force is a strange "sideways" push — it never speeds a charge up or slows it down, only bends its path, like a string swinging a ball in a circle. That perpendicular shove is what spins motors and curves particle beams.

The Right-Hand Rule and Electromagnetism

Right-hand rule
Point your right hand's fingers along the velocity (or current), curl toward the field B, and your thumb gives the force direction (for a positive charge). It is the standard way to find the direction of magnetic force.

Crucially, moving charges create magnetic fields too — a current in a wire is surrounded by a magnetic field. Electricity and magnetism are unified into electromagnetism, and accelerating charges produce electromagnetic waves: light.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — force on a moving charge
A charge of 2 C moves at 3 m/s perpendicular to a 0.5 T magnetic field. Find the magnetic force.
1
F = qvB = 2 × 3 × 0.5.
F = 3 N, perpendicular to both the velocity and the field.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — force on a wire
A 0.4 m wire carries 5 A through a 0.2 T field (perpendicular). Find the force on it.
1
F = BIL = 0.2 × 5 × 0.4.
F = 0.4 N.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A 3 C charge moves at 4 m/s perpendicular to a 2 T field. Find the magnetic force. (F = qvB.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

F = qvB = 3 × 4 × 2 = 24 N.

F = 24 N
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. A 0.6 m wire carries 10 A perpendicular to a 0.3 T field. Find the force on the wire. (F = BIL.) Work below.
Show worked solution

F = BIL = 0.3 × 10 × 0.6 = 1.8 N.

F = 1.8 N
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 3. Does a charge sitting still in a magnetic field feel a magnetic force? Why or why not? Explain below.
Show worked solution

No. The magnetic force is F = qvB, which is zero when v = 0. A charge must be moving to feel a magnetic force.

No — magnetic force requires motion (F = qvB = 0 if v = 0)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work — it changes a charge's direction, never its speed. And only moving charges feel it (and create magnetic fields); a stationary charge has no magnetic interaction.

Key Takeaways
  • Force on a moving charge: F = qvB (perpendicular to v and B); zero if not moving.
  • Force on a current-carrying wire: F = BIL — the basis of motors.
  • The right-hand rule gives the force direction; the force does no work (only bends paths).
  • Moving charges create magnetic fields — electromagnetism unifies the two, and light is an EM wave.
📊 FIGURE — poles, and making electricity from magnetism
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Two poles, and why they always come in pairs

Every magnet has a north and a south pole, and the rule matches the electric one: like poles repel, opposite poles attract. Bring two north poles together and they push apart; north to south and they pull together.

The difference from electricity is that you can isolate a positive charge, but you cannot isolate a north pole. Cut a bar magnet in half and you do not get a north piece and a south piece — you get two complete magnets, each with its own north and south. Keep cutting and it keeps happening. No magnetic monopole has ever been observed.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Faraday’s law: turning a changing field into voltage

A magnetic field sitting still does nothing. A changing magnetic flux Φ through a loop induces an EMF (a voltage) around it — that is Faraday’s law: EMF = −N ΔΦ/Δt.

Let the flux through a loop fall from 0.40 Wb to 0.10 Wb over 0.20 s:

|EMF| = |0.10 - 0.40| / 0.20 = 1.5 V with N = 200 turns: 300.0 V
computed with NumPy 2.4.6

One loop gives 1.5 V; winding 200 turns multiplies it to 300 V. That is a generator: spin a coil so the flux through it keeps changing, and you get voltage out.

The minus sign is Lenz’s law — the induced current flows in whichever direction opposes the change that created it. Push a magnet toward a coil and the coil pushes back; that resistance is exactly the work you feel turning a generator.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Expecting a steady magnetic field to induce a current. It induces nothing. Only a changing flux does — change the field strength, the loop area, or the angle. A magnet resting on a coil produces zero EMF.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Three ways to change Φ = BA cosθ, and exam questions use all three: change B (move the magnet), change A (squeeze the loop), or change θ (rotate it — this is how real generators work).

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Ohm's law and the rules for combining resistors are the foundation of all circuit analysis — phones, computers, appliances, the power grid. These few relationships let you predict current, voltage, and power anywhere in a circuit.

Current is the flow of charge; resistance opposes it; and voltage drives it. Ohm's law ties them together, and simple rules handle resistors in series and parallel.

Current, Voltage, Resistance

Electric current
I = Q/t — charge flowing per unit time, measured in amperes (1 A = 1 C/s).
Ohm's law
V = I·R — voltage equals current times resistance (R in ohms, Ω). More voltage drives more current; more resistance reduces it.
Electric power
P = I·V (also P = I²R) — the rate energy is delivered, in watts. This is what your electric bill measures.
Figure 1. A basic circuit: a battery provides voltage, driving current around the loop through a resistor R. Ohm's law (V = IR) relates the three.

Resistors in Series and Parallel

ArrangementTotal resistance
Series (end to end)R = R₁ + R₂ + … (adds up)
Parallel (side by side)1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … (total is less than the smallest)
🧠 ANALOGY

Think water pipes: voltage is the pump pressure, current is the flow rate, resistance is a narrow section. Series resistors are narrow pipes in a row (each adds restriction). Parallel resistors are extra pipes side by side — more paths means easier flow, so less total resistance.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — Ohm's law
A 12 V battery drives current through a 4 Ω resistor. Find the current.
1
V = IR, so I = V/R = 12/4.
I = 3 A.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — power
A device draws 2 A at 120 V. Find the power it uses.
1
P = IV = 2 × 120.
P = 240 W.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A 9 V battery is connected to a 3 Ω resistor. Find the current. (I = V/R.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

I = V/R = 9/3 = 3 A.

I = 3 A
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 5 Ω are connected in series. Find the total resistance. Work below.
Show worked solution

Series resistances add: R = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 Ω.

R = 10 Ω
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 3. A 24 V battery drives a circuit with total resistance 6 Ω. Find the current, then the power delivered (P = IV). Work below.
Show worked solution

I = V/R = 24/6 = 4 A. P = IV = 4 × 24 = 96 W.

I = 4 A; P = 96 W
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Series and parallel rules are opposite: series resistances add, but parallel ones combine through reciprocals and give a total smaller than any single resistor. Mixing up the two formulas is the most common circuit error.

Key Takeaways
  • Current: I = Q/t (amperes); Ohm's law: V = IR.
  • Power: P = IV (watts).
  • Series: resistances add. Parallel: 1/R = Σ 1/Rᵢ (total < smallest).
  • Voltage drives current; resistance opposes it.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Voltage — electric potential — is the quantity your batteries, outlets, and devices are all rated in. It measures the energy available to push charges through a circuit, making it the most practical electrical concept of all.

Electric potential (voltage) is electric potential energy per unit charge. It tells you how much energy each coulomb of charge carries, and differences in potential are what drive current through circuits.

Electric Potential and Energy

Electric potential
V = kq/r is the potential (in volts) a distance r from a point charge. The potential energy of a charge q at potential V is U = qV. One volt = one joule per coulomb.
Uniform field relation
In a uniform field (like between parallel plates), the potential difference relates to the field by V = E·d, where d is the distance along the field.
🧠 ANALOGY

Voltage is like height in a water system: water flows from high to low, and charges flow from high to low potential. A battery is a pump that lifts charge to high "voltage height"; the circuit lets it flow back down, doing work (lighting a bulb) along the way.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — potential energy
A charge of 3 C is moved to a point where the potential is 12 V. Find its electric potential energy.
1
U = qV = 3 × 12.
U = 36 J.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — field between plates
Two parallel plates are 0.02 m apart with a 100 V potential difference. Find the electric field between them.
1
V = E·d, so E = V/d = 100/0.02.
E = 5000 V/m (equivalently 5000 N/C).
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A charge of 5 C sits at a point with potential 9 V. Find its electric potential energy. (U = qV.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

U = qV = 5 × 9 = 45 J.

U = 45 J
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. Two plates 0.05 m apart have a 200 V difference. Find the electric field between them. (E = V/d.) Work below.
Show worked solution

E = V/d = 200/0.05 = 4000 V/m.

E = 4000 V/m
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Do not confuse electric potential (V, volts — energy per charge) with potential energy (U, joules — the total). They are related by U = qV. Potential is a property of a location in the field; potential energy belongs to a specific charge sitting there.

Key Takeaways
  • Electric potential (voltage) = potential energy per charge: V = kq/r; 1 V = 1 J/C.
  • Potential energy: U = qV.
  • In a uniform field, V = E·d.
  • Charges flow from high to low potential, like water downhill.
📊 FIGURE — equipotential surfaces
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Mapping the potential around a point charge

An equipotential is the set of all points sitting at the same potential. Since V = kq/r depends only on the distance r, every point the same distance from a point charge has the same V — so the equipotentials are spheres centred on the charge.

For q = 5 nC:

r = 0.30 m -> V = 149.833 V r = 0.60 m -> V = 74.9167 V
computed with NumPy 2.4.6

Every point on the 0.30 m sphere sits at 149.8 V. Slide a charge anywhere around that sphere and ΔV = 0, so the work done is W = qΔV = 0.

That zero is what forces the geometry. If the field had any component along the surface it would do work as the charge slid along — but the work is zero, so the field can have no such component. The field must cross every equipotential at exactly 90°.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Reading "equipotential" as "no field". The potential is constant along the surface, but the field is generally strong there — it just points straight across it. Note also that doubling r from 0.30 to 0.60 m halves V (149.8 → 74.9), because potential falls as 1/r — not as 1/r², which is the field.
🎯 EXAM TIP
On a map of field lines, equipotentials are the contour lines — and like a hiking map, closely spaced contours mean a steep slope, which here means a strong field.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Electric charge and the forces between charges underlie all of electricity, chemistry, and electronics. Coulomb's law quantifies the attraction and repulsion that holds atoms together and drives every circuit — the electrical counterpart to Newton's gravity.

Electric charge comes in two kinds, positive and negative. Like charges repel, opposites attract, and Coulomb's law gives the strength of that force. The electric field describes the influence a charge spreads through space.

Coulomb's Law

Coulomb's law
F = k·q₁·q₂ / r², where q₁ and q₂ are the charges (in coulombs), r is the distance between them, and k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². The force is along the line joining the charges: repulsive for like charges, attractive for opposite.
🧠 ANALOGY

Coulomb's law looks just like Newton's gravity — both fall off as 1/r². But charge comes in two signs (so the force can attract or repel), while mass has only one (gravity only attracts). Electric forces are also vastly stronger.

The Electric Field

Electric field
The electric field E = F/q is the force per unit charge at a point (units: N/C). A field from a point charge is E = kq/r². Field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative ones.
Figure 1. Electric field lines radiate outward from a positive charge (inward for negative). A positive test charge placed in the field feels a force along the line.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — Coulomb's law
Two charges of 2 × 10⁻⁶ C and 3 × 10⁻⁶ C are 0.5 m apart. Find the force between them. (k = 8.99 × 10⁹)
1
F = k·q₁·q₂/r² = (8.99 × 10⁹)(2 × 10⁻⁶)(3 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.5²).
2
Numerator: (8.99 × 10⁹)(6 × 10⁻¹²) = 5.39 × 10⁻². Divide by 0.25.
F ≈ 0.216 N, repulsive (both charges positive).
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 1. Two charges are a distance r apart. If the distance is halved, what happens to the electric force between them? Explain below.
Show worked solution

F ∝ 1/r². Halving r makes r² one-quarter as large, so the force becomes 4 times stronger.

The force becomes 4× stronger
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. Find the electric field magnitude E = kq/r² at 0.2 m from a charge of 4 × 10⁻⁶ C. (k = 8.99 × 10⁹.) Work below.
Show worked solution

E = kq/r² = (8.99 × 10⁹)(4 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.2²) = (3.596 × 10⁴)/(0.04) ≈ 8.99 × 10⁵ N/C.

E ≈ 9.0 × 10⁵ N/C
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Charges are tiny in coulombs — typically microcoulombs (10⁻⁶ C). Keep careful track of the powers of ten, and remember r is squared. Like Coulomb's law itself, the field is an inverse-square quantity.

Key Takeaways
  • Like charges repel, opposites attract; Coulomb's law: F = kq₁q₂/r².
  • It is an inverse-square law (like gravity), but charge comes in two signs.
  • Electric field: E = F/q = kq/r²; lines point away from +, toward −.
  • k = 8.99 × 10⁹; charges are usually in microcoulombs.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The ideal gas law connects pressure, volume, and temperature in one equation, explaining everything from why tires gain pressure on hot days to how engines and weather work. Kinetic theory reveals that all of it comes from countless tiny molecular collisions.

Kinetic theory pictures a gas as a swarm of tiny particles in constant random motion. Their collisions with the walls create pressure, and their average speed sets the temperature. The ideal gas law ties the macroscopic quantities together.

The Ideal Gas Law

Ideal gas law
PV = nRT, where P is pressure, V is volume, n is the number of moles, R = 8.31 J/(mol·K) is the gas constant, and T is the absolute temperature (in kelvin). It links all the state variables of a gas.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
🧠 ANALOGY

A gas is like a room full of bouncing rubber balls hammering the walls. Each impact is a tiny push; together they make pressure. Heat the room and the balls move faster, hitting harder and more often — raising pressure (or expanding the volume). That is kinetic theory.

The Simple Gas Laws

LawRelationship (fixed amount)
Boyle'sP ∝ 1/V at constant T (squeeze → higher pressure)
Charles'sV ∝ T at constant P (heat → expand)
Gay-Lussac'sP ∝ T at constant V (heat → higher pressure)
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — ideal gas law
Find the pressure of 2 moles of gas in a 0.05 m³ container at 300 K. (R = 8.31)
1
Solve PV = nRT for P: P = nRT/V.
2
P = (2)(8.31)(300)/(0.05) = 4986/0.05.
P ≈ 99,720 Pa (about atmospheric pressure).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — Boyle's law
A gas at 100 kPa occupies 2 L. If compressed to 1 L at the same temperature, what is the new pressure?
1
Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ → (100)(2) = P₂(1).
2
200 = P₂.
P₂ = 200 kPa — halving the volume doubles the pressure.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Find the pressure of 1 mole of gas in a 0.025 m³ container at 273 K. (P = nRT/V, R = 8.31.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

P = nRT/V = (1)(8.31)(273)/(0.025) = 2268.6/0.025 ≈ 90,744 Pa.

P ≈ 90,700 Pa
✐ PRACTICE — challenge (Boyle's law)
Problem 2. A gas at 200 kPa occupies 3 L. It is compressed to 1.5 L at constant temperature. Find the new pressure. (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.) Work below.
Show worked solution

(200)(3) = P₂(1.5) → 600 = 1.5 P₂ → P₂ = 400 kPa.

P₂ = 400 kPa
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The ideal gas law requires temperature in kelvin, not Celsius — using °C (or worse, a negative °C) gives nonsense. Always convert: K = °C + 273 before plugging into PV = nRT.

Key Takeaways
  • Kinetic theory: gas pressure comes from molecular collisions; temperature from average molecular speed.
  • Ideal gas law: PV = nRT (T in kelvin, R = 8.31).
  • Boyle's (P ∝ 1/V), Charles's (V ∝ T), Gay-Lussac's (P ∝ T).
  • Always use kelvin for temperature in gas calculations.

Zeroth lawtemperature via thermal equilibrium.
Second lawentropy never decreases; heat flows hot → cold; no perfect engine.

Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The laws of thermodynamics govern energy, engines, refrigerators, and the direction of time itself. They tell us energy is conserved, why heat flows one way, and why perfect efficiency is impossible — among the most profound and practical laws in all of science.

Four laws summarize how energy and heat behave. The first is energy conservation; the second introduces entropy and the arrow of time. Together they shape everything thermal.

The Laws

Zeroth Law
If two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other. This is what makes temperature a consistent, measurable quantity.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
First Law (energy conservation)
ΔU = Q − W: the change in a system's internal energy equals the heat added minus the work it does. Energy is conserved — it only changes form.
Second Law (entropy)
The total entropy (disorder) of an isolated system never decreases. Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never the reverse, and no engine can be perfectly efficient.
Third Law
As temperature approaches absolute zero (0 K), entropy approaches a minimum. Absolute zero can be approached but never actually reached.
🧠 ANALOGY

The second law is why a shuffled deck never spontaneously sorts itself, and a hot coffee always cools to room temperature (never the reverse). Disorder naturally increases; reversing it always takes outside effort. That one-way tendency is the arrow of time.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — first law
A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work. Find the change in its internal energy.
1
First law: ΔU = Q − W.
2
ΔU = 500 − 200.
ΔU = 300 J — the internal energy increased by 300 J.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A system absorbs 800 J of heat and does 300 J of work. Find ΔU. (ΔU = Q − W.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

ΔU = Q − W = 800 − 300 = 500 J.

ΔU = 500 J
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. Why does a hot cup of coffee left on a table always cool down, rather than spontaneously getting hotter? Which law explains this? Explain below.
Show worked solution

The second law: heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold (increasing total entropy). The coffee transfers heat to the cooler room until they reach equilibrium; the reverse would decrease entropy and never happens on its own.

The second law — heat flows hot → cold, entropy increases
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

In the first law ΔU = Q − W, mind the signs: Q is positive when heat is added to the system, and W is positive when the system does work on its surroundings. Getting these sign conventions backwards flips the answer.

Key Takeaways
  • Zeroth law defines temperature via thermal equilibrium.
  • First law: ΔU = Q − W (energy conservation).
  • Second law: entropy never decreases; heat flows hot → cold; no perfect engine.
  • Third law: absolute zero is unreachable.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Temperature and heat are distinct ideas often confused in everyday speech. Getting them straight — and learning how much energy it takes to warm something (specific heat) — is the basis of all thermal physics, from cooking to climate to engines.

Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles; heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. They are related but not the same — a key distinction.

Temperature vs Heat

Temperature
Temperature reflects the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance. Scales: Celsius (°C), Kelvin (K, where 0 K is absolute zero), and Fahrenheit (°F). Note K = °C + 273.
Heat
Heat Q is energy in transit from a hotter object to a cooler one. It is measured in joules. Heat flows until both reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium).
🧠 ANALOGY

A lit match and a warm bathtub: the match flame is at a far higher temperature, but the tub holds far more total thermal energy (it could melt more ice). Temperature is "how hot per particle"; heat is the energy that actually moves between things.

Specific Heat

Specific heat
The heat needed to change a substance's temperature: Q = mcΔT, where m is mass, c is the specific heat (energy per kg per degree), and ΔT is the temperature change. Water has a famously high c, so it heats and cools slowly.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — heat to warm water
How much heat is needed to raise 2 kg of water by 10°C? (c_water = 4186 J/kg·°C)
1
Q = mcΔT = (2)(4186)(10).
2
= 2 × 4186 × 10 = 83,720.
Q = 83,720 J ≈ 83.7 kJ. (Water's high specific heat means it takes a lot of energy.)
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. How much heat raises 0.5 kg of water by 20°C? (c = 4186 J/kg·°C, Q = mcΔT.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

Q = mcΔT = (0.5)(4186)(20) = 41,860 J ≈ 41.9 kJ.

Q ≈ 41,860 J
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. Convert 25°C to Kelvin. (K = °C + 273.) Work below.
Show worked solution

K = 25 + 273 = 298 K.

298 K
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Temperature and heat are not the same thing. A large object at low temperature can contain more heat energy than a tiny object at high temperature. Temperature is intensive (per particle); heat is extensive (total energy transferred).

Key Takeaways
  • Temperature = average kinetic energy of particles; heat = energy transferred by a temperature difference.
  • Scales: K = °C + 273; absolute zero is 0 K.
  • Specific heat: Q = mcΔT.
  • Water's high specific heat makes it slow to heat and cool.

Direction of heat flow: heat naturally flows from hot to cold — never spontaneously the other way. This is distinct from pressure and volume, which describe a gas state, not heat transfer.

📊 FIGURE — the three ways heat travels
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature

Heat moves in exactly three ways. Conduction passes energy particle-to-particle through a material. Convection carries it in the bulk motion of a fluid — warm air rising, cool air sinking. Radiation sends it as electromagnetic waves, which is why the Sun heats us across empty space.

The conduction rate through a slab is Q/t = kAΔT / L, where k is the thermal conductivity. Take A = 2 m², ΔT = 20 °C, L = 0.05 m:

wood (k = 0.08): 64.0 W copper (k = 400): 320000.0 W ratio: 5000.0
computed with NumPy 2.4.6

Same slab, same temperature difference — copper moves heat 5000× faster.

That number answers the classic question. A metal doorknob and a wooden door in the same room are at the same temperature. The metal feels colder because its high conductivity conducts heat away from your hand far faster. You are not sensing temperature at all — you are sensing how quickly heat leaves your skin.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Saying "cold flows into my hand". Cold is not a substance and nothing flows inward. Heat flows out of your hand, from hot to cold, and the sensation of cold is the rate of that outward flow.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Match the mode to the medium: solid contact → conduction; a moving liquid or gas → convection; across a vacuum or as glow → radiation. Radiation is the only one that needs no medium at all.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Sound is the wave we live inside — speech, music, sonar, ultrasound imaging. Understanding it as a longitudinal pressure wave explains pitch, loudness, echoes, and the everyday Doppler effect you hear when a siren passes.

Sound is a longitudinal wave: a traveling pattern of compressions and rarefactions in a medium like air. Its wave properties translate directly into what we hear — pitch and loudness.

What Sound Is

Sound waves
Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave — air molecules vibrate back and forth along the direction of travel, creating regions of compression and rarefaction. It needs a medium (no sound in a vacuum).
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

In air at room temperature, sound travels at about 343 m/s. It moves faster in liquids and faster still in solids, where molecules are more tightly coupled.

Pitch and Loudness

We perceiveWave property
Pitch (high/low)Frequency (high f = high pitch)
LoudnessAmplitude (bigger = louder)
🧠 ANALOGY

Sound is like a Slinky push: shove one end and a compression travels down the coils while each coil just jiggles in place. Air does the same — passing the squeeze along to your ear. A faster jiggle (higher frequency) sounds higher-pitched.

The Doppler Effect

Doppler effect
When a sound source moves toward you, the waves bunch up → higher pitch; moving away, they stretch out → lower pitch. This is why a passing siren drops in pitch as it goes by.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — wavelength of sound
A sound wave in air (v = 343 m/s) has a frequency of 686 Hz. Find its wavelength.
1
Use v = f·λ, so λ = v/f = 343/686.
λ = 0.5 m.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A sound wave travels at 343 m/s with frequency 1000 Hz. Find its wavelength. (λ = v/f) Show your work.
Show worked solution

λ = v/f = 343/1000 = 0.343 m.

λ ≈ 0.343 m
✐ PRACTICE — challenge (echo timing)
Problem 2. You shout at a cliff and hear the echo 2 s later. How far away is the cliff? (Sound travels at 343 m/s; remember the sound goes there AND back.) Work below.
Show worked solution

Total distance traveled = v·t = 343 × 2 = 686 m. That is the round trip, so the cliff is half: 686/2 = 343 m away.

343 m
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 3. As an ambulance with its siren on speeds toward you and then away, how does the pitch you hear change? Explain below.
Show worked solution

Approaching, the waves bunch up, so you hear a higher pitch. After it passes and recedes, the waves stretch out, so the pitch drops to lower. This is the Doppler effect.

Higher pitch approaching, then lower pitch receding (Doppler effect)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Sound needs a medium — there is no sound in the vacuum of space. And in echo problems, remember the sound travels to the surface and back, so the distance to the object is half the total path. Don't forget the round trip.

Key Takeaways
  • Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave; ~343 m/s in air, faster in solids/liquids.
  • Pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude.
  • Doppler effect: approaching → higher pitch, receding → lower pitch.
  • Sound needs a medium; echoes involve a round trip (halve the distance).

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Waves carry energy without carrying matter — light, sound, water ripples, seismic waves, radio. The handful of properties that describe all waves (wavelength, frequency, speed) form the vocabulary for optics, acoustics, and communications.

A wave is a traveling disturbance that transports energy. A few quantities describe every wave, and one simple equation ties speed, frequency, and wavelength together.

The Anatomy of a Wave

PropertyMeaning
Wavelength (λ)Distance between successive crests (meters)
Frequency (f)Cycles passing a point per second (hertz)
AmplitudeMaximum displacement (height) — relates to energy
Period (T)Time for one cycle; T = 1/f
Figure 1. Wavelength λ is the crest-to-crest distance; amplitude is the height from the rest line. Frequency counts how many wavelengths pass per second.

The Wave Equation and Wave Types

Wave speed
v = f·λ — wave speed equals frequency times wavelength. For a fixed medium, v is constant, so higher frequency means shorter wavelength.
Transverse vs longitudinal
Transverse: the medium moves perpendicular to the wave's travel (light, waves on a string). Longitudinal: the medium moves parallel to the travel, as compressions (sound).
🧠 ANALOGY

A wave is like "the wave" in a stadium: energy and the pattern travel around the arena, but each person just stands up and sits down — no one runs around the stadium. The disturbance moves; the medium stays put.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — wave speed
A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 4 m. Find its speed.
1
v = f·λ = 50 × 4.
v = 200 m/s.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A wave has frequency 20 Hz and wavelength 3 m. Find its speed. Show your work.
Show worked solution

v = f·λ = 20 × 3 = 60 m/s.

v = 60 m/s
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. A wave travels at 340 m/s with a frequency of 170 Hz. Find its wavelength. (Rearrange v = fλ to λ = v/f.) Work below.
Show worked solution

λ = v/f = 340/170 = 2 m.

λ = 2 m
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

A wave transports energy, not matter — the medium oscillates in place and does not travel with the wave. Also, amplitude relates to a wave's energy/intensity, while frequency and wavelength are independent of it.

Key Takeaways
  • Waves carry energy without carrying matter.
  • Key properties: wavelength λ, frequency f, amplitude, period T = 1/f.
  • Wave speed: v = f·λ.
  • Transverse (perpendicular) vs longitudinal (parallel) motion.
📊 FIGURE — when two waves overlap
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Adding two waves, and where each kind happens

Superposition is the whole rule: where two waves overlap, the displacement at each point is the sum of what each wave would do on its own.

Take waves of amplitude 3 cm and 2 cm:

  • Crest meeting crest — they reinforce: 3 + 2 = 5 cm. That is constructive interference.
  • Crest meeting trough — they oppose: |3 − 2| = 1 cm. That is destructive interference. Had both been 3 cm, the result would be exactly 0 — complete cancellation.

Which one you get depends on the path difference — how much further one wave travelled. With λ = 2 m:

path diff 1.0 m = 0.5 lambda -> destructive path diff 2.0 m = 1.0 lambda -> constructive path diff 3.0 m = 1.5 lambda -> destructive path diff 4.0 m = 2.0 lambda -> constructive
computed with NumPy 2.4.6

A whole number of wavelengths puts the waves back in step (constructive); a half-odd number puts them exactly out of step (destructive).

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Believing destructive interference destroys energy. It does not — energy is conserved. The wave is cancelled at that point and reinforced somewhere else; the dark and bright bands of an interference pattern are the same energy redistributed, not energy lost.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Two rules cover almost every exam question: path difference = mλ → constructive; path difference = (m + ½)λ → destructive. Count in wavelengths, not metres.

The pendulum is the classic timekeeper — its steady period built the first accurate clocks. And tracking how energy flows between kinetic and potential during oscillation deepens the conservation-of-energy ideas into the world of vibrations.

A pendulum swings in simple harmonic motion (for small angles), with a period that depends only on its length and gravity. Throughout any oscillation, energy sloshes between kinetic and potential forms.

The Pendulum Period

Pendulum period
For small swings, a pendulum of length L has period T = 2π√(L/g). Remarkably, it does not depend on the mass of the bob or (for small angles) the amplitude — only on length and gravity.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
🧠 ANALOGY

A long pendulum swings lazily; a short one ticks quickly — which is why a grandfather clock's pendulum is about a meter long to give a satisfying one-second-ish swing. Adjusting the length is how you tune such a clock.

Energy in SHM

Energy exchange
In SHM, total energy is constant but continuously converts: maximum kinetic energy at equilibrium (fastest point) and maximum potential energy at the extremes (turning points, momentarily at rest). KE + PE stays fixed.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — pendulum period
Find the period of a pendulum 1 m long. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
1
T = 2π√(L/g) = 2π√(1/9.8) = 2π√(0.102).
2
√0.102 ≈ 0.319, so T = 2π(0.319) ≈ 2.0.
T ≈ 2.0 s. (A 1 m pendulum swings once about every 2 seconds.)
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Find the period of a 0.25 m pendulum. (T = 2π√(L/g), g = 9.8.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

T = 2π√(0.25/9.8) = 2π√(0.0255) ≈ 2π(0.16) ≈ 1.0 s.

T ≈ 1.0 s
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 2. At which point in a pendulum's swing is its kinetic energy greatest, and where is its potential energy greatest? Explain below.
Show worked solution

Kinetic energy is greatest at the bottom (equilibrium), where it moves fastest. Potential energy is greatest at the highest points of the swing (the turning points), where it momentarily stops.

KE max at the bottom; PE max at the extremes
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The simple pendulum formula T = 2π√(L/g) holds only for small angles (roughly under 15°). For large swings, the motion is no longer perfectly simple harmonic and the period grows slightly. Also, the bob's mass does not appear — heavier bobs swing with the same period.

Key Takeaways
  • Pendulum period: T = 2π√(L/g) — depends only on length and gravity (small angles).
  • Mass and (small) amplitude do not affect the period.
  • In SHM, energy converts between KE (max at center) and PE (max at extremes).
  • Total mechanical energy stays constant throughout.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is the universal pattern of vibration — masses on springs, atoms in solids, AC circuits, even the swaying of buildings. Master this one repeating motion and you understand oscillations everywhere in nature and engineering.

Simple harmonic motion happens whenever a restoring force pulls an object back toward equilibrium in proportion to its displacement. The result is a smooth, repeating back-and-forth motion described by sines and cosines.

The Restoring Force

Simple harmonic motion
SHM occurs when the restoring force obeys F = −kx (Hooke's law): the force is proportional to displacement x and points back toward equilibrium (the minus sign). This produces sinusoidal oscillation.
Figure 1. In SHM, position traces a sine curve in time, swinging between +A and −A (the amplitude). The motion repeats with a fixed period.

Period and Frequency

Period of a mass-spring system
The time for one full cycle is T = 2π√(m/k), where m is the mass and k the spring constant. The frequency f = 1/T (cycles per second, in hertz) is how many oscillations occur each second.
🧠 ANALOGY

A mass on a spring is like a ball rolling back and forth in a valley — always pulled toward the bottom (equilibrium), overshooting, then pulled back. A stiffer spring (bigger k) is a steeper valley, so it oscillates faster; a heavier mass sloshes more slowly.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — period of a spring
A 2 kg mass is attached to a spring with k = 8 N/m. Find the period of oscillation.
1
T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π√(2/8) = 2π√(0.25).
2
√0.25 = 0.5, so T = 2π(0.5) = π.
T = π ≈ 3.14 s per cycle.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A 4 kg mass is on a spring with k = 16 N/m. Find the period. (T = 2π√(m/k)) Show your work.
Show worked solution

T = 2π√(4/16) = 2π√(0.25) = 2π(0.5) = π ≈ 3.14 s.

T = π ≈ 3.14 s
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. An oscillator completes one cycle every 0.25 s. Find its frequency. (f = 1/T) Work below.
Show worked solution

f = 1/T = 1/0.25 = 4 Hz (4 cycles per second).

f = 4 Hz
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The period of a mass-spring system depends on mass and spring stiffness — not on the amplitude. Pull the mass farther and it still takes the same time per cycle (it just moves faster). This amplitude-independence is a hallmark of SHM.

Key Takeaways
  • SHM arises from a restoring force F = −kx (proportional to displacement, opposing it).
  • Motion is sinusoidal, swinging between +A and −A.
  • Period: T = 2π√(m/k); frequency: f = 1/T.
  • Period is independent of amplitude.

Newton's law of universal gravitation explains the falling apple and the orbiting Moon with one equation — a landmark unification in science. It governs planets, tides, satellites, and the structure of the cosmos, and it is the foundation of orbital mechanics.

Every mass attracts every other mass. Newton's law of gravitation says the force grows with the masses and falls off with the square of the distance between them.

The Law of Gravitation

Universal gravitation
F = G·m₁·m₂ / r², where m₁ and m₂ are the masses, r is the distance between their centers, and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² is the gravitational constant. The force is attractive and acts along the line joining them.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
🧠 ANALOGY

Gravity is the same force whether it pulls an apple to the ground or holds the Moon in orbit — Newton's great insight. The Moon is just "falling" toward Earth continuously, but moving sideways fast enough that it keeps missing, circling instead of hitting.

Surface Gravity

Surface gravity
The acceleration due to gravity at a distance r from a planet of mass M is g = GM/r². This is why g ≈ 9.8 m/s² at Earth's surface, and weaker on smaller or less massive worlds.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — gravitational force
Find the gravitational force between two 1000 kg masses whose centers are 2 m apart. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)
1
F = G·m₁·m₂/r² = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(1000)(1000)/(2²).
2
= (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(10⁶)/4 = (6.67 × 10⁻⁵)/4.
F ≈ 1.67 × 10⁻⁵ N — gravity between everyday objects is extremely weak.
💡 TIP — the inverse-square law

Because of the r² in the denominator, doubling the distance makes gravity one-quarter as strong; tripling it makes it one-ninth. This rapid weakening with distance is the signature of an inverse-square law.

✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 1. If the distance between two masses is doubled, what happens to the gravitational force between them? Explain below.
Show worked solution

F ∝ 1/r². Doubling r makes r² four times larger, so the force becomes 1/4 of its original value.

The force becomes 1/4 as strong
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. Find the surface gravity g = GM/r² for a planet of mass M = 6 × 10²⁴ kg and radius r = 6.4 × 10⁶ m. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹) Work below.
Show worked solution

g = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(6 × 10²⁴)/(6.4 × 10⁶)². Numerator ≈ 4.0 × 10¹⁴. Denominator = (6.4 × 10⁶)² ≈ 4.1 × 10¹³. g ≈ 4.0 × 10¹⁴ / 4.1 × 10¹³ ≈ 9.8 m/s². (This is Earth!)

g ≈ 9.8 m/s²
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The r in the formula is the distance between centers, not surfaces. For an object on Earth's surface, r is Earth's radius (~6,400 km), not zero. And the inverse-square means force drops fast — but never reaches exactly zero at any finite distance.

Key Takeaways
  • Universal gravitation: F = G·m₁·m₂/r², attractive between all masses.
  • It is an inverse-square law — double the distance, quarter the force.
  • Surface gravity: g = GM/r² (gives 9.8 m/s² for Earth).
  • r is measured between centers; the same law governs apples and orbits.

Angular momentum is the rotational version of momentum, and like momentum it is conserved. This single principle explains spinning skaters, the stability of bicycles and tops, and even why galaxies and hurricanes rotate the way they do.

Angular momentum is "rotational inertia in motion" — the product of moment of inertia and angular velocity. With no external torque, it is conserved, leading to some striking effects.

Angular Momentum and Its Conservation

Angular momentum
L = Iω — moment of inertia times angular velocity. Units: kg·m²/s. It is the rotational analog of linear momentum p = mv.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
Conservation of angular momentum
With no net external torque, L is constant: Iω stays the same. So if I decreases, ω must increase to compensate (and vice versa).
🧠 ANALOGY

A spinning figure skater pulls their arms in and suddenly whirls faster — no push needed. Pulling the arms in lowers the moment of inertia I, so to keep L = Iω constant, ω shoots up. Stretch the arms back out and the spin slows again. That is conservation of angular momentum you can see.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — angular momentum
A wheel has moment of inertia 4 kg·m² and spins at 5 rad/s. Find its angular momentum.
1
L = Iω = 4 × 5.
L = 20 kg·m²/s.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — conservation (skater)
A skater with I = 6 kg·m² spins at 2 rad/s, then pulls in to I = 2 kg·m². Find the new angular velocity.
1
Angular momentum is conserved: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂.
2
(6)(2) = (2)ω₂ → 12 = 2ω₂.
3
ω₂ = 6 rad/s.
ω₂ = 6 rad/s — pulling in (lower I) tripled the spin rate.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A disk with moment of inertia 3 kg·m² spins at 8 rad/s. Find its angular momentum. Show your work.
Show worked solution

L = Iω = 3 × 8 = 24 kg·m²/s.

L = 24 kg·m²/s
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. A spinning platform with I = 10 kg·m² at 3 rad/s has its moment of inertia reduced to 5 kg·m². Using conservation of angular momentum, find the new angular velocity. Work below.
Show worked solution

I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂ → (10)(3) = (5)ω₂ → 30 = 5ω₂ → ω₂ = 6 rad/s.

ω₂ = 6 rad/s
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Angular momentum is conserved only when there is no external torque. The skater speeds up not because of any push, but because lowering I forces ω up to keep L fixed — energy is not the conserved quantity here, angular momentum is.

Key Takeaways
  • Angular momentum: L = Iω, the rotational analog of p = mv.
  • Conserved when no external torque acts: Iω stays constant.
  • Lower I → higher ω (and vice versa) — the spinning-skater effect.
  • Explains tops, gyroscopes, and rotational stability.

Torque is the rotational version of force — what makes things spin. Moment of inertia is rotational mass — resistance to spinning. Together they give the rotational form of Newton's second law, explaining everything from why door handles are far from the hinge to how flywheels store energy.

Torque is a twisting force that causes rotation; it depends on how far from the axis you push and at what angle. Moment of inertia measures how hard an object is to spin up. They combine in τ = Iα.

Torque

Torque
τ = r·F·sin θ, where r is the distance from the axis to where the force is applied, F is the force, and θ is the angle between them. Maximum torque comes from pushing perpendicular (θ = 90°), far from the axis. Units: N·m.
Figure 1. Torque = force × lever arm. Pushing farther from the axis (larger r) or perpendicular (θ = 90°) produces more turning effect — why long wrenches loosen tight bolts.

Moment of Inertia and Rotational Newton's Law

Moment of inertia
I is rotational mass — resistance to angular acceleration. It depends on both mass and how that mass is distributed: mass farther from the axis gives larger I. For a point mass, I = mr².
Rotational Newton's Second Law
τ = Iα — net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration, the rotational twin of F = ma.
🧠 ANALOGY

A figure skater spins faster when pulling their arms in — same mass, but now closer to the axis, lowering the moment of inertia. And a door is easy to swing from the handle (large r, large torque) but nearly impossible to push near the hinge (tiny r). Distance from the axis is everything.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — torque
A force of 20 N is applied perpendicular to a wrench 0.3 m from the bolt. Find the torque.
1
Perpendicular means θ = 90°, sin 90° = 1.
2
τ = r·F·sin θ = 0.3 × 20 × 1.
τ = 6 N·m.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — rotational Newton's law
A net torque of 10 N·m acts on a wheel with moment of inertia 5 kg·m². Find its angular acceleration.
1
τ = Iα, so α = τ/I = 10/5.
α = 2 rad/s².
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A 15 N force is applied perpendicular to a door 0.8 m from the hinge. Find the torque. Show your work.
Show worked solution

τ = r·F·sin 90° = 0.8 × 15 × 1 = 12 N·m.

τ = 12 N·m
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. A net torque of 24 N·m acts on a disk with moment of inertia 8 kg·m². Find the angular acceleration. Work below.
Show worked solution

α = τ/I = 24/8 = 3 rad/s².

α = 3 rad/s²
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Torque depends on the lever arm (distance from the axis) and the angle, not just the force. The same force gives more torque farther out and zero torque if applied straight toward the axis (θ = 0). Moment of inertia depends on mass distribution, not just total mass.

Key Takeaways
  • Torque: τ = r·F·sin θ — the rotational "force," maximized perpendicular and far from the axis.
  • Moment of inertia I is rotational mass; depends on mass distribution (I = mr² for a point mass).
  • τ = Iα is the rotational Newton's second law.
  • Mass farther from the axis is harder to spin.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Wheels, gears, planets, and motors all rotate, and rotational motion has its own complete set of quantities and equations — perfectly parallel to straight-line motion. Learning the analogy once unlocks all of rotational mechanics.

Rotational motion mirrors linear motion with new variables: angle θ replaces position, angular velocity ω replaces velocity, and angular acceleration α replaces acceleration. The same kinematic equations apply, with rotational symbols.

The Rotational Quantities

LinearRotationalUnits
position xangle θradians
velocity vangular velocity ωrad/s
acceleration aangular acceleration αrad/s²

The Rotational Kinematic Equations

Rotational kinematics
For constant angular acceleration: ω = ω₀ + αt, θ = ω₀t + ½αt², and ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ — identical in form to the linear equations.
📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

Linking Rotation to Linear Motion

Linear-angular connection
A point at radius r from the axis moves with linear speed v = rω and tangential acceleration a = rα. Farther from the axis means faster linear motion for the same rotation.
🧠 ANALOGY

On a spinning merry-go-round, everyone shares the same angular velocity ω (one full turn together). But a child near the edge whips around with high linear speed (v = rω) while one near the center barely moves. Same rotation, different linear speeds by radius.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — angular velocity
A wheel starts from rest and accelerates at 2 rad/s² for 3 s. Find its final angular velocity.
1
Use ω = ω₀ + αt with ω₀ = 0.
2
ω = 0 + (2)(3).
ω = 6 rad/s.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — linear speed of a point
A point sits 0.5 m from the axis of a wheel spinning at ω = 4 rad/s. Find its linear speed.
1
v = rω = 0.5 × 4.
v = 2 m/s.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A disk starts from rest and accelerates at 3 rad/s² for 4 s. Find its final angular velocity. Show your work.
Show worked solution

ω = ω₀ + αt = 0 + 3(4) = 12 rad/s.

ω = 12 rad/s
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. A point 2 m from the axis rotates at ω = 5 rad/s. Find its linear speed. Work below.
Show worked solution

v = rω = 2 × 5 = 10 m/s.

v = 10 m/s
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Angular quantities use radians, not degrees, in these equations (one full revolution = 2π radians ≈ 6.28). Plugging in degrees breaks the v = rω relationship. Convert to radians first.

Key Takeaways
  • Rotational motion uses θ, ω, α in place of x, v, a.
  • The kinematic equations have identical form (ω = ω₀ + αt, etc.).
  • Linear-angular link: v = rω, a = rα.
  • Always work in radians.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

From billiard balls to car crashes to subatomic particles, collisions are everywhere — and conservation of momentum lets you predict their outcomes even without knowing the messy forces involved. This is one of physics' most practical and elegant tools.

In any collision with no outside forces, the total momentum is conserved — the momentum before equals the momentum after. Whether kinetic energy is also conserved distinguishes elastic from inelastic collisions.

Conservation of Momentum

Momentum conservation
For an isolated system, total p before = total p after: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = m₁v₁′ + m₂v₂′. The internal collision forces are equal and opposite (third law), so they cancel out.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

Elastic vs Inelastic

TypeMomentumKinetic energy
ElasticConservedConserved (bounce apart)
InelasticConservedNot conserved (some lost to heat/sound)
Perfectly inelasticConservedMaximum loss (objects stick together)
🧠 ANALOGY

Two superballs colliding bounce apart with almost no energy lost — nearly elastic. Two lumps of clay smacking together and sticking — perfectly inelastic, with energy going into deforming the clay. Momentum is conserved in both; only the bounciness (kinetic energy) differs.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — perfectly inelastic collision
A 2 kg cart moving at 3 m/s strikes and sticks to a stationary 1 kg cart. Find their common velocity afterward.
1
Momentum before: (2)(3) + (1)(0) = 6 kg·m/s.
2
They stick, so afterward they move together with combined mass 3 kg at velocity v′: 3v′ = 6.
3
v′ = 6/3 = 2 m/s.
They move off together at 2 m/s. (Momentum conserved; some kinetic energy was lost in sticking.)
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A 4 kg cart moving at 5 m/s collides and sticks to a 1 kg stationary cart. Find their common velocity afterward. Show your work.
Show worked solution

Momentum before = (4)(5) + (1)(0) = 20 kg·m/s. Combined mass = 5 kg. 5v′ = 20 → v′ = 4 m/s.

v′ = 4 m/s
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. A 3 kg ball moving at 4 m/s collides head-on with a 3 kg ball moving at −2 m/s (opposite direction). They stick together. Find the final velocity. Work below.
Show worked solution

Momentum before = (3)(4) + (3)(−2) = 12 − 6 = 6 kg·m/s. Combined mass = 6 kg. 6v′ = 6 → v′ = 1 m/s (in the positive direction).

v′ = 1 m/s
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Momentum is conserved in every collision, but kinetic energy is not conserved in inelastic ones — do not assume energy conservation unless the collision is elastic. And momentum is a vector: include signs for objects moving in opposite directions.

Key Takeaways
  • Total momentum is conserved in all collisions (isolated system).
  • Elastic: kinetic energy also conserved; inelastic: some KE lost.
  • Perfectly inelastic: objects stick together (maximum KE loss).
  • Use signs for opposite directions; do not assume KE is conserved.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Momentum measures "quantity of motion" and is conserved in collisions — making it the key to analyzing crashes, rocket propulsion, and recoil. Impulse explains why airbags and crumple zones save lives: they change momentum gently over more time.

Momentum is mass in motion — the product of mass and velocity. Impulse is what changes momentum: a force applied over a time. They are linked by the impulse-momentum theorem.

Momentum and Impulse

Momentum
p = mv — a vector pointing in the direction of motion. Units: kg·m/s. A heavy slow truck and a light fast bullet can have similar momentum.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
Impulse
J = F·Δt = Δp. A force F acting for time Δt delivers an impulse equal to the change in momentum. Spreading the same momentum change over more time means less force.
🧠 ANALOGY

Catching a fast ball, you pull your hands back — extending the stopping time so the force on your hand is gentler. Same momentum change, more time, less force. That is exactly why airbags and crumple zones work: they lengthen Δt to shrink the force.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — momentum
Find the momentum of a 1000 kg car moving at 15 m/s.
1
p = mv = 1000 × 15.
p = 15,000 kg·m/s in the direction of motion.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — impulse changes momentum
A 0.5 kg ball moving at 4 m/s is stopped. What impulse was applied?
1
Impulse = change in momentum = Δp = p_f − p₀.
2
p₀ = 0.5 × 4 = 2 kg·m/s; p_f = 0. So Δp = 0 − 2 = −2 kg·m/s.
Impulse = −2 kg·m/s (or 2 N·s opposite the motion).
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Find the momentum of a 70 kg runner moving at 8 m/s. Show your work.
Show worked solution

p = mv = 70 × 8 = 560 kg·m/s.

p = 560 kg·m/s
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. A force of 20 N acts on an object for 3 s. Find the impulse, which equals the change in momentum. Work below.
Show worked solution

J = F·Δt = 20 × 3 = 60 N·s (= 60 kg·m/s change in momentum).

J = 60 N·s
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 3. A 2 kg ball moving at 5 m/s is brought to rest by a force acting over 0.4 s. Find the average force. (First find Δp, then use F = Δp/Δt.) Work below.
Show worked solution

Δp = 0 − (2)(5) = −10 kg·m/s. F = Δp/Δt = −10/0.4 = −25 N (25 N opposing the motion).

F = −25 N (magnitude 25 N)
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Momentum is a vector — direction (and sign) matters. A ball that bounces back has a larger momentum change than one that just stops, because its velocity reverses (from +v to −v, a change of 2v, not just v). Always track the signs.

Key Takeaways
  • Momentum: p = mv (a vector), measured in kg·m/s.
  • Impulse: J = F·Δt = Δp (the change in momentum).
  • More time for the same Δp means less force (airbags, crumple zones).
  • Momentum is a vector — track direction and sign, especially for bounces.

TermDefinition
Conservation of energyone of the deepest laws in all of science — energy is never created or destroyed, only transformed.
Potential energystored energy — energy of position or configuration.
ConservationKE + PE = constant (with no friction).
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Conservation of energy is one of the deepest laws in all of science — energy is never created or destroyed, only transformed. Combined with potential energy, it lets you solve motion problems (like a roller coaster's speed) in one line, without ever touching forces or acceleration.

Potential energy is stored energy — energy of position or configuration. As an object moves, energy converts between potential and kinetic, but (without friction) the total stays constant.

Two Common Potential Energies

Gravitational PE
Energy stored by height: PE = mgh, where h is the height above a reference level. Lift something up and you store this energy; it is released as it falls.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
Elastic (spring) PE
Energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring: PE = ½kx², where k is the spring constant and x the displacement from the natural length.

Conservation of Mechanical Energy

Conservation of energy
With no friction, the total mechanical energy is constant: KE + PE = constant. Equivalently, KE₀ + PE₀ = KE_f + PE_f. Energy just shifts between kinetic and potential forms.
🧠 ANALOGY

A roller coaster trades height for speed: slow and high at the top (lots of PE), fast and low at the bottom (lots of KE). The total never changes — every bit of height "spent" becomes speed, and vice versa. That is conservation of energy in action.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — gravitational PE
A 3 kg book is placed on a shelf 2 m high. Find its gravitational potential energy. (g = 9.8)
1
PE = mgh = 3 × 9.8 × 2.
PE = 58.8 J relative to the floor.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — conservation: find the speed
An object is dropped from a height of 5 m. How fast is it moving just before it hits the ground? (Use energy conservation, g = 9.8.)
1
At the top: all PE, no KE. At the bottom: all KE, no PE. So mgh = ½mv² (mass cancels).
2
gh = ½v² → v² = 2gh = 2 × 9.8 × 5 = 98.
3
v = √98 ≈ 9.9 m/s.
v ≈ 9.9 m/s — and notice the mass never mattered.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A 5 kg rock sits at the top of a 10 m cliff. Find its gravitational potential energy. (g = 9.8) Show your work.
Show worked solution

PE = mgh = 5 × 9.8 × 10 = 490 J.

PE = 490 J
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. A ball is dropped from a height of 20 m. Using energy conservation (v² = 2gh), find its speed just before impact. (g = 9.8) Work below.
Show worked solution

v² = 2gh = 2 × 9.8 × 20 = 392. v = √392 ≈ 19.8 m/s.

v ≈ 19.8 m/s
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 3. A spring with k = 200 N/m is compressed 0.1 m. How much elastic potential energy is stored? (PE = ½kx²) Work below.
Show worked solution

PE = ½kx² = ½(200)(0.1²) = ½(200)(0.01) = 1 J.

PE = 1 J
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Energy conservation in the simple form KE + PE = constant assumes no friction (or other energy losses). When friction is present, some mechanical energy converts to heat, so KE₀ + PE₀ = KE_f + PE_f + (energy lost to friction).

Key Takeaways
  • Gravitational PE: mgh; elastic PE: ½kx².
  • Conservation: KE + PE = constant (with no friction).
  • Energy converts between kinetic and potential; the total is preserved.
  • In free fall, v² = 2gh — independent of mass.

TermDefinition
Energyone of the most powerful ideas in physics — it is conserved, so tracking it solves problems that forces alone make messy.
Workwhat a force does when it moves an object through a distance, and it transfers
Kinetic energyKE = ½mv² — scales with speed squared.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Energy is one of the most powerful ideas in physics — it is conserved, so tracking it solves problems that forces alone make messy. The link between work and kinetic energy is where the energy approach begins, turning force-times-distance into motion.

Work is what a force does when it moves an object through a distance, and it transfers energy. Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. The two are tied together by the work-energy theorem.

Work

Work
W = F·d·cos θ, where F is the force, d the distance moved, and θ the angle between them. Units: joules (1 J = 1 N·m). A force perpendicular to the motion (θ = 90°) does zero work.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

Kinetic Energy

Kinetic energy
The energy of a moving object: KE = ½mv². It grows with the square of speed — double the speed, quadruple the energy. Units: joules.
Work-Energy Theorem
The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔKE = ½mv² − ½mv₀². Do positive work and it speeds up; do negative work (like friction) and it slows.
🧠 ANALOGY

Work is like depositing energy into an object's "motion account," and kinetic energy is the balance. Push it forward (positive work) and the balance grows; friction makes withdrawals (negative work) until the account — and the motion — runs down.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — work done by a force
A 50 N force pushes a box 4 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done?
1
Force and motion are aligned, so θ = 0 and cos 0 = 1.
2
W = F·d·cos θ = 50 × 4 × 1.
W = 200 J.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — kinetic energy
Find the kinetic energy of a 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s.
1
KE = ½mv² = ½(2)(3²) = ½(2)(9).
KE = 9 J.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A 30 N force drags a crate 6 m in the direction of the force. Find the work done. Show your work.
Show worked solution

W = F·d·cos 0 = 30 × 6 × 1 = 180 J.

W = 180 J
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. Find the kinetic energy of a 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s. Work below.
Show worked solution

KE = ½mv² = ½(1000)(20²) = ½(1000)(400) = 200,000 J = 200 kJ.

KE = 200,000 J
✐ PRACTICE — challenge (work-energy theorem)
Problem 3. A 4 kg object speeds up from 2 m/s to 6 m/s. How much net work was done on it? (Use W = ½mv² − ½mv₀².) Work below.
Show worked solution

Final KE = ½(4)(6²) = ½(4)(36) = 72 J. Initial KE = ½(4)(2²) = ½(4)(4) = 8 J. W_net = 72 − 8 = 64 J.

W_net = 64 J
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Only the component of force along the motion does work — that is the cos θ factor. A force perpendicular to motion (like the normal force, or gravity on a horizontally moving object) does zero work. And kinetic energy uses v squared, so it is always positive.

Key Takeaways
  • Work: W = F·d·cos θ (joules); perpendicular forces do no work.
  • Kinetic energy: KE = ½mv² — scales with speed squared.
  • Work-energy theorem: W_net = ΔKE.
  • Positive work speeds up, negative work (friction) slows down.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Anything moving in a circle — a car rounding a curve, a satellite orbiting, a ball on a string — is constantly accelerating, even at constant speed. Understanding centripetal force explains why, and is essential for orbits, turns, and rotating machinery.

An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating, because its direction keeps changing. That acceleration points toward the center, and producing it requires a center-directed centripetal force.

Centripetal Acceleration and Force

Centripetal acceleration
An object moving at speed v in a circle of radius r has acceleration a = v²/r directed toward the center. "Centripetal" means "center-seeking."
Centripetal force
The net inward force needed is F = ma = mv²/r. This is not a new kind of force — it is provided by tension, gravity, friction, or whatever physically points toward the center.
Figure 1. The velocity (green) points along the circle (tangent), while the centripetal force (red) points toward the center. The force constantly bends the path into a circle.
🧠 ANALOGY

Swing a ball on a string in a circle: the string pulls it inward, constantly bending its path. Let go — the inward force vanishes and the ball flies off in a straight line (tangent), not outward. There is no real "outward" force; the inward pull is what keeps it circling.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — centripetal acceleration
A car rounds a curve of radius 50 m at 20 m/s. Find its centripetal acceleration.
1
a = v²/r = (20)²/50.
2
= 400/50.
a = 8 m/s², directed toward the center of the curve.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — centripetal force
A 2 kg ball on a string moves in a circle of radius 1 m at 4 m/s. Find the tension (the centripetal force).
1
F = mv²/r = 2 × (4²)/1 = 2 × 16/1.
F = 32 N — the string tension provides this inward force.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A runner moves around a circular track of radius 25 m at 5 m/s. Find the centripetal acceleration. Show your work.
Show worked solution

a = v²/r = 5²/25 = 25/25 = 1 m/s².

a = 1 m/s²
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. A 1000 kg car rounds a curve of radius 40 m at 10 m/s. Find the centripetal force needed (this must be supplied by friction). Work below.
Show worked solution

F = mv²/r = 1000 × (10²)/40 = 1000 × 100/40 = 1000 × 2.5 = 2500 N.

F = 2500 N
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Centripetal force is not a separate force you add to a diagram — it is the net inward force, supplied by real forces like tension, gravity, or friction. And there is no outward "centrifugal force" on the object; the outward feeling is just inertia resisting the inward turn.

Key Takeaways
  • Circular motion at constant speed still accelerates (direction changes).
  • Centripetal acceleration: a = v²/r, toward the center.
  • Centripetal force: F = mv²/r, supplied by tension/gravity/friction.
  • It is the net inward force, not a new force; there is no real outward force.

📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Frictionforce that lets you walk, drive, and grip — and the force that slows everything down.
Kinetic frictionf_k = μ_k N (during sliding), opposing motion.
Static frictionf_s ≤ μ_s N (before sliding), matching the applied push up to its max.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Friction is the force that lets you walk, drive, and grip — and the force that slows everything down. Quantifying it is essential for realistic mechanics, from designing brakes to predicting whether a box will slide. It is the most common "extra" force in real problems.

Friction opposes sliding between surfaces. It comes in two flavors: static friction (preventing motion from starting) and kinetic friction (acting once sliding begins). Both depend on how hard the surfaces press together.

Static vs Kinetic Friction

Kinetic friction
Once an object slides, kinetic friction has magnitude f_k = μ_k N, where μ_k is the coefficient of kinetic friction and N is the normal force. It points opposite the motion.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
Static friction
Before sliding, static friction matches whatever push is applied, up to a maximum f_s ≤ μ_s N. Exceed that maximum and the object breaks free and starts to slide.
🧠 ANALOGY

Static friction is like a stubborn box that refuses to budge until you push hard enough — it pushes back exactly as much as you push, until it gives. Kinetic friction is the steady drag you feel once it is sliding, usually a bit weaker than the initial "stuck" resistance.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — kinetic friction force
A 10 kg box slides across a floor with μ_k = 0.3. Find the kinetic friction force. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
1
On a flat floor, the normal force balances weight: N = mg = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N.
2
f_k = μ_k N = 0.3 × 98.
f_k = 29.4 N, opposing the motion.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — maximum static friction
A 5 kg block rests on a surface with μ_s = 0.4. What is the most horizontal force it can take before sliding? (g = 9.8)
1
N = mg = 5 × 9.8 = 49 N.
2
Maximum static friction: f_s(max) = μ_s N = 0.4 × 49 = 19.6 N.
It can resist up to 19.6 N; any push beyond that starts it sliding.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A 20 kg crate slides with μ_k = 0.25. Find the kinetic friction force. (g = 9.8) Show your work.
Show worked solution

N = mg = 20 × 9.8 = 196 N. f_k = μ_k N = 0.25 × 196 = 49 N.

f_k = 49 N
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. A 6 kg box is pushed with 40 N horizontally; μ_k = 0.2. Find the friction force, then the net force and acceleration. (g = 9.8) Work below.
Show worked solution

N = mg = 6 × 9.8 = 58.8 N. f_k = 0.2 × 58.8 = 11.76 N. Net force = 40 − 11.76 = 28.24 N. a = 28.24/6 ≈ 4.71 m/s².

f_k ≈ 11.8 N; net ≈ 28.2 N; a ≈ 4.71 m/s²
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Friction depends on the normal force, not the object's weight directly — they are equal only on a flat surface with no vertical push. On an incline, N is smaller than mg, so friction is too. Also, static friction is "up to" its max — it is not always at maximum.

Key Takeaways
  • Kinetic friction: f_k = μ_k N (during sliding), opposing motion.
  • Static friction: f_s ≤ μ_s N (before sliding), matching the applied push up to its max.
  • Friction depends on the normal force N, not weight directly.
  • Static friction's maximum usually exceeds kinetic friction.

📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
free-body diagramsingle most important problem-solving tool in mechanics.
Weight (mg)Always straight down
Normal (N)Perpendicular to the surface, pushing away
Tension (T)Along a rope, pulling away from the object
Friction (f)Along the surface, opposing motion
Applied (F)Whatever push or pull is given
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A free-body diagram is the single most important problem-solving tool in mechanics. By drawing every force acting on one object, you turn a confusing word problem into a clear set of equations. Nearly every force problem starts with one.

A free-body diagram isolates one object and shows all the forces acting on it as arrows. Once drawn, you apply Newton's second law (ΣF = ma) separately in the horizontal and vertical directions.

Common Forces to Include

ForceDirection
Weight (mg)Always straight down
Normal (N)Perpendicular to the surface, pushing away
Tension (T)Along a rope, pulling away from the object
Friction (f)Along the surface, opposing motion
Applied (F)Whatever push or pull is given
Figure 1. A free-body diagram of a box being pushed: weight (down), normal force (up), applied force (right), friction (left). All arrows start at the object and point in the force's direction.
🧠 ANALOGY

A free-body diagram is like a tug-of-war snapshot for one object: draw every rope pulling on it and how hard. Whichever direction "wins" (has more net force) is the direction it accelerates. If the pulls balance, it stays put or coasts.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — box at rest on a table
A 5 kg box sits on a table. Find the normal force on it. (Use g = 9.8 m/s².)
1
Forces: weight down (mg) and normal up (N). The box is not accelerating, so ΣF = 0 vertically.
2
N − mg = 0 → N = mg = 5 × 9.8.
N = 49 N upward.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — net force and acceleration
A 10 kg box is pushed with 40 N right while 10 N of friction acts left. Find its acceleration.
1
Net horizontal force: ΣF = 40 − 10 = 30 N (to the right).
2
a = ΣF/m = 30/10.
a = 3 m/s² to the right.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A 8 kg object hangs at rest from a rope. What is the tension in the rope? (At rest, tension balances weight; g = 9.8.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

At rest, T = mg = 8 × 9.8 = 78.4 N.

T = 78.4 N
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 2. A 4 kg box is pushed right with 30 N; friction of 6 N opposes it. Find the net force and the acceleration. Work below.
Show worked solution

Net force = 30 − 6 = 24 N right. a = F/m = 24/4 = 6 m/s².

Net force = 24 N; a = 6 m/s²
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Draw only forces acting on the object — never forces the object exerts on other things. And the normal force is not always equal to mg; on an incline or when there is a vertical push/pull, you must recompute it from the vertical force balance.

Key Takeaways
  • A free-body diagram shows all forces acting on a single isolated object.
  • Common forces: weight, normal, tension, friction, applied.
  • Apply ΣF = ma separately in the x and y directions.
  • Include only forces on the object; the normal force ≠ mg in general.

📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Newton's three lawsfoundation of all classical mechanics.
First lawno net force → no change in motion (inertia).
Second lawF = ma (net force = mass × acceleration).
Third lawforces come in equal, opposite pairs acting on different objects.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Newton's three laws are the foundation of all classical mechanics. They explain why objects start, stop, and change direction — from a rocket launch to a car crash to walking across a room. Master these three statements and you can analyze almost any everyday motion.

In the late 1600s, Newton distilled all of motion into three laws. The first defines what force does, the second says how much, and the third reveals that forces always come in pairs.

The Three Laws

First Law (Inertia)
An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity, unless acted on by a net external force. Objects resist changes to their motion — that resistance is inertia.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
Second Law (F = ma)
The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration: F = ma. More force means more acceleration; more mass means less. Force is measured in newtons (1 N = 1 kg·m/s²).
Third Law (Action-Reaction)
For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. If A pushes on B with some force, B pushes back on A with an equal force in the opposite direction.
🧠 ANALOGY

First law: a hockey puck glides forever on frictionless ice until something stops it. Second law: pushing an empty cart speeds it up fast, a loaded cart slowly. Third law: step off a small boat and the boat shoots backward as you step forward — you pushed it, it pushed you.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — apply F = ma
A net force of 12 N acts on a 3 kg object. Find its acceleration.
1
Use F = ma, solve for a: a = F/m.
2
a = 12 N / 3 kg.
a = 4 m/s².
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — find the force
What net force gives a 1500 kg car an acceleration of 2 m/s²?
1
F = ma = 1500 × 2.
F = 3000 N.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A net force of 50 N acts on a 10 kg cart. Find its acceleration. Show your work.
Show worked solution

a = F/m = 50/10 = 5 m/s².

a = 5 m/s²
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. What net force is needed to accelerate a 2 kg ball at 8 m/s²? Work below.
Show worked solution

F = ma = 2 × 8 = 16 N.

F = 16 N
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 3. A book rests on a table. By the third law, the table pushes up on the book. What is the equal-and-opposite partner force, and what does it act on? Explain below.
Show worked solution

The reaction partner is the book pushing down on the table with an equal force. Action-reaction pairs always act on different objects (book on table, table on book).

The book pushes down on the table with equal force
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

F = ma uses the net force (the sum of all forces), not a single force. And action-reaction pairs act on different objects — so they never cancel each other out (the book's weight and the table's normal force are not a third-law pair, since both act on the book).

Key Takeaways
  • First law: no net force → no change in motion (inertia).
  • Second law: F = ma (net force = mass × acceleration).
  • Third law: forces come in equal, opposite pairs acting on different objects.
  • Always use the net force in F = ma.

📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Projectile motiona thrown ball, a launched arrow, water from a hose — combines everything from this chapter.
Vertical (y)−g (9.8 m/s² down)
Horizontalconstant velocity (a = 0).
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Projectile motion — a thrown ball, a launched arrow, water from a hose — combines everything from this chapter. The crucial insight, that horizontal and vertical motion are completely independent, makes these problems tractable and reveals why projectiles trace parabolas.

A projectile moves under gravity alone after launch. The key principle: its horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Horizontally it coasts at constant velocity; vertically it is in free fall.

The Two Independent Motions

DirectionAccelerationBehavior
Horizontal (x)0Constant velocity: x = vₓt
Vertical (y)−g (9.8 m/s² down)Free fall: y = v_y₀t − ½gt²

Time t is the link between them — it is the same in both directions.

Figure 1. A projectile's path is a parabola. At the peak, the vertical velocity is momentarily zero, but the horizontal velocity never changes throughout the flight.
🧠 ANALOGY

Drop a ball and fire another horizontally at the same instant from the same height — they hit the ground together. Gravity pulls both down identically; the fired one's horizontal motion does not delay its fall. Vertical and horizontal motion truly do not affect each other.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — horizontal launch
A ball rolls off a 1.96 m high table at 5 m/s horizontally. How long until it lands, and how far away?
1
Vertical (find time to fall): 1.96 = ½gt² = ½(9.8)t² = 4.9t². So t² = 0.4 → t = 0.632 s.
2
Horizontal (constant velocity): x = vₓt = 5 × 0.632.
Time ≈ 0.63 s; horizontal distance ≈ 3.16 m. (The horizontal speed never affected the fall time.)
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — components of an angled launch
A projectile is launched at 20 m/s at 30°. Find its initial horizontal and vertical velocity components.
1
vₓ = 20 cos 30° = 20(0.866) ≈ 17.3 m/s (stays constant the whole flight).
2
v_y₀ = 20 sin 30° = 20(0.5) = 10 m/s (decreases under gravity).
vₓ ≈ 17.3 m/s, v_y₀ = 10 m/s.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A ball rolls off a table and takes 0.5 s to hit the floor. How high is the table? (Use y = ½gt², g = 9.8.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

y = ½gt² = ½(9.8)(0.5²) = ½(9.8)(0.25) = 1.225 m.

height = 1.225 m
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. A projectile is launched at 40 m/s at 60°. Find its horizontal and vertical velocity components. (cos 60° = 0.5, sin 60° ≈ 0.866.) Work below.
Show worked solution

vₓ = 40 cos 60° = 40(0.5) = 20 m/s. v_y₀ = 40 sin 60° = 40(0.866) ≈ 34.6 m/s.

vₓ = 20 m/s, v_y₀ ≈ 34.6 m/s
✐ PRACTICE — challenge
Problem 3. A ball is thrown horizontally at 8 m/s from a 4.9 m high ledge. How far horizontally does it travel before landing? (First find the fall time from 4.9 = ½gt².) Work below.
Show worked solution

4.9 = ½(9.8)t² = 4.9t² → t² = 1 → t = 1 s. Horizontal: x = vₓt = 8(1) = 8 m.

x = 8 m
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Never mix the horizontal and vertical equations together. Gravity affects only the vertical motion; the horizontal velocity is constant. Solve each direction separately and use the shared time to connect them.

Key Takeaways
  • A projectile's horizontal and vertical motions are independent.
  • Horizontal: constant velocity (a = 0). Vertical: free fall (a = −g).
  • The path is a parabola; at the peak v_y = 0 but vₓ is unchanged.
  • Time links the two directions — solve each separately.
