◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Real motion is rarely along a straight line. Vectors let you handle motion (and forces) in two or three dimensions by splitting them into independent components. This decomposition trick is one of the most powerful problem-solving moves in all of physics.

A vector has both magnitude and direction. The key skill is breaking a vector into perpendicular components (x and y), handling each direction separately, then recombining.

Components of a Vector

Vector components
A vector of magnitude V at angle θ above the horizontal splits into Vₓ = V cos θ (horizontal) and V_y = V sin θ (vertical). To rebuild: magnitude V = √(Vₓ² + V_y²), and direction θ = arctan(V_y/Vₓ).
Figure 1. A vector V at angle θ resolves into a horizontal piece Vₓ = V cos θ and a vertical piece V_y = V sin θ. The two components are independent.
🧠 ANALOGY

Walking diagonally across a city is the same as walking some blocks east and some blocks north. Any diagonal move breaks cleanly into an east-west part and a north-south part — and you can deal with each grid direction on its own. That is vector decomposition.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — resolve a vector
A velocity of 10 m/s points 30° above the horizontal. Find its components.
1
Horizontal: Vₓ = V cos θ = 10 cos 30° = 10(0.866).
2
Vertical: V_y = V sin θ = 10 sin 30° = 10(0.5).
Vₓ ≈ 8.66 m/s, V_y = 5 m/s.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — magnitude from components
A vector has components Vₓ = 3, V_y = 4. Find its magnitude.
1
V = √(Vₓ² + V_y²) = √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25.
V = 5 (with direction θ = arctan(4/3) ≈ 53° above horizontal).
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A force of 20 N points at 60° above the horizontal. Find its x and y components. (cos 60° = 0.5, sin 60° ≈ 0.866.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

Fₓ = 20 cos 60° = 20(0.5) = 10 N. F_y = 20 sin 60° = 20(0.866) ≈ 17.3 N.

Fₓ = 10 N, F_y ≈ 17.3 N
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. A vector has components (6, 8). Find its magnitude. Work below.
Show worked solution

V = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10.

V = 10
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Match the trig function to the angle's reference. With θ measured from the horizontal, the horizontal component uses cosine and the vertical uses sine. If the angle is measured from the vertical instead, these swap — always check what the angle is measured from.

Key Takeaways
  • A vector has magnitude and direction; resolve it into perpendicular components.
  • From the horizontal: Vₓ = V cos θ, V_y = V sin θ.
  • Recombine with V = √(Vₓ² + V_y²) and θ = arctan(V_y/Vₓ).
  • The x and y directions are independent — handle them separately.
📊 FIGURE — multiplying a vector by a number
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Scaling one vector three ways

Start from v = (3, 4), whose magnitude is √(3² + 4²) = 5, pointing about 53.1° above the horizontal.

import numpy as np
v = np.array([3., 4.])
for s in (2, -2, 0.5):
    w = s * v
    print(s, w, np.linalg.norm(w),
          np.degrees(np.arctan2(w[1], w[0])))
2 [6. 8.] 10.0 53.1301 -2 [-6. -8.] 10.0 -126.8699 0.5 [1.5 2. ] 2.5 53.1301
computed with NumPy 2.4.6
  • 2v = (6, 8), magnitude 10 — twice as long, and the angle is unchanged at 53.1°. Same direction, double the size.
  • −2v = (−6, −8), magnitude also 10. The length doubled, but the angle flipped to −126.9°, which is exactly 53.1° + 180°. That is the reversal.
  • 0.5v = (1.5, 2), magnitude 2.5 — half as long, direction untouched.

So multiplying by −2 does two separate things at once: it doubles the length (that is the 2) and reverses the direction (that is the minus sign).

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Thinking a negative scalar gives a negative length. Magnitude is never negative — the new magnitude is |s| × |v|, using the absolute value of the scalar. The minus sign spends itself entirely on the direction, flipping the vector 180°.
🎯 EXAM TIP
To scale a vector, multiply each component by the scalar — there is no trigonometry involved. The angle only ever does one of two things: stay the same (s > 0) or turn 180° (s < 0).

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

When acceleration is constant — a braking car, a dropped ball, a launched rocket in its burn — four kinematic equations predict everything about the motion. These are among the most-used formulas in all of physics, and free fall is their most famous application.

If acceleration stays constant, the motion is fully described by four equations relating position, velocity, acceleration, and time. Pick the one containing your knowns and the unknown you want.

The Four Kinematic Equations

EquationLeaves out
v = v₀ + atposition
x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at²final velocity
v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀)time
x = x₀ + ½(v₀ + v)tacceleration

Here v₀ is the initial velocity, v the final velocity, a the (constant) acceleration, and t the time.

Figure 1. On a velocity-time graph, the slope is acceleration and the area under the line is displacement. Constant acceleration gives a straight line.
🧠 ANALOGY

The four equations are like four tools in a kit, each missing one variable. If a problem never mentions time, grab the timeless one (v² = v₀² + 2aΔx). Matching the tool to what you know and want is the whole skill.

Free Fall

Free fall
Near Earth's surface, gravity gives every object the same downward acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (often rounded to 10). Just substitute a = g (or −g, depending on your sign choice) into the kinematic equations.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — accelerating car
A car starts from rest (v₀ = 0) and accelerates at 3 m/s² for 5 s. How far does it travel?
1
Knowns: v₀ = 0, a = 3, t = 5; want x. Use x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² (leaves out final velocity).
2
x = 0 + (0)(5) + ½(3)(5²) = ½(3)(25).
x = 37.5 m.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — dropped object
A ball is dropped from rest. How fast is it moving after 2 s? (Use g = 9.8 m/s².)
1
Knowns: v₀ = 0, a = g = 9.8, t = 2; want v. Use v = v₀ + at.
2
v = 0 + (9.8)(2).
v = 19.6 m/s downward.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A cyclist starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 6 s. Find the final velocity and the distance traveled. Show your work.
Show worked solution

v = v₀ + at = 0 + 2(6) = 12 m/s. x = ½at² = ½(2)(36) = 36 m.

v = 12 m/s; x = 36 m
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. A ball is dropped from rest. How far has it fallen after 3 s? (Use g = 9.8 m/s², x = ½gt².) Work below.
Show worked solution

x = ½gt² = ½(9.8)(3²) = ½(9.8)(9) = 44.1 m.

x = 44.1 m
✐ PRACTICE — challenge (timeless equation)
Problem 3. A car traveling at 20 m/s brakes at −4 m/s² until it stops (v = 0). How far does it travel? (Use v² = v₀² + 2a·Δx.) Work below.
Show worked solution

0 = 20² + 2(−4)Δx → 0 = 400 − 8Δx → 8Δx = 400 → Δx = 50 m.

Δx = 50 m
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Pick a sign convention for direction and stick with it. If "up" is positive, then gravity gives a = −9.8 m/s². Mixing signs mid-problem (or forgetting the negative on a downward acceleration) is the most common source of wrong answers.

Key Takeaways
  • For constant acceleration, four kinematic equations relate x, v, a, and t.
  • Choose the equation that omits the variable you do not have.
  • Free fall: a = g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward for all objects.
  • On a v-t graph, slope = acceleration and area = displacement.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Every physics problem about motion starts here. Position, velocity, and acceleration are the three quantities that describe how things move — and getting their precise meanings (and the difference between distance and displacement) right is what separates correct physics from confused physics.

Motion is described by three linked quantities: position (where something is), velocity (how fast and which way it moves), and acceleration (how its velocity changes). Each is the rate of change of the one before it.

Position and Displacement

Displacement vs distance
Displacement Δx is the change in position — a vector (has direction), measured straight from start to finish. Distance is the total path length — a scalar (no direction). Walk 3 m east then 3 m west: distance = 6 m, displacement = 0.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

Velocity and Acceleration

Velocity
Velocity = displacement ÷ time, a vector. Average velocity = Δx/Δt. Its magnitude is speed (a scalar). Units: m/s.
Acceleration
Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time = Δv/Δt, a vector. Units: m/s². A negative acceleration can mean slowing down or speeding up in the negative direction.
🧠 ANALOGY

Your car's odometer measures distance (always increasing); a straight line from home to work measures displacement. The speedometer shows speed; add "heading north" and you have velocity. Pressing the gas or brake changes velocity — that change is acceleration.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — average velocity
A runner moves from x = 2 m to x = 22 m in 5 seconds. Find the average velocity.
1
Displacement: Δx = 22 − 2 = 20 m.
2
Average velocity = Δx/Δt = 20 m / 5 s.
v = 4 m/s in the positive direction.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — acceleration
A car speeds up from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 4 seconds. Find its acceleration.
1
Change in velocity: Δv = 30 − 10 = 20 m/s.
2
a = Δv/Δt = 20 m/s ÷ 4 s.
a = 5 m/s² — the velocity increases by 5 m/s every second.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. A cyclist travels from x = 5 m to x = 65 m in 10 s. Find the average velocity. Show your work.
Show worked solution

Δx = 65 − 5 = 60 m. v = Δx/Δt = 60/10 = 6 m/s.

v = 6 m/s
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. A train slows from 25 m/s to 5 m/s in 8 s. Find its acceleration (watch the sign). Work below.
Show worked solution

Δv = 5 − 25 = −20 m/s. a = −20/8 = −2.5 m/s². The negative sign means it is decelerating.

a = −2.5 m/s²
✐ PRACTICE — concept
Problem 3. A person walks 8 m east, then 5 m west. What is the total distance traveled, and what is the displacement? Work below.
Show worked solution

Distance = 8 + 5 = 13 m (total path). Displacement = 8 − 5 = 3 m east (straight-line net change).

Distance = 13 m; displacement = 3 m east
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Distance and displacement are not the same, and neither are speed and velocity. Distance and speed are scalars (no direction); displacement and velocity are vectors. Always track direction with a sign (+ or −) in one-dimensional problems.

Key Takeaways
  • Displacement (vector) is the net change in position; distance (scalar) is total path length.
  • Velocity = Δx/Δt (vector); its magnitude is speed.
  • Acceleration = Δv/Δt (vector); negative does not always mean "slowing."
  • Track direction with signs in 1-D motion.

📋 Newton's Laws & Forces

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Newton's Three Laws

▸ First Law (Inertia) An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity, unless acted on by a net external force . Objects resist changes to their motion — that resistance is inertia .

▸ Second Law (F = ma) The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration: F = ma . More force means more acceleration; more mass means less. Force is measured in newtons (1 N = 1 kg·m/s²).

▸ Third Law (Action-Reaction) For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction . If A pushes on B with some force, B pushes back on A with an equal force in the opposite direction.

Free-Body Diagrams

Common Forces to Include — Figure 1. A free-body diagram of a box being pushed: weight (down), normal force (up), applied force (right), friction (left). All arrows start at the object and point…

Friction

▸ Kinetic friction Once an object slides, kinetic friction has magnitude f_k = μ_k N , where μ_k is the coefficient of kinetic friction and N is the normal force. It points opposite the motion.

▸ Static friction Before sliding, static friction matches whatever push is applied, up to a maximum f_s ≤ μ_s N . Exceed that maximum and the object breaks free and starts to slide.

Circular Motion

▸ Centripetal acceleration An object moving at speed v in a circle of radius r has acceleration a = v²/r directed toward the center. "Centripetal" means "center-seeking."

▸ Centripetal force The net inward force needed is F = ma = mv²/r . This is not a new kind of force — it is provided by tension, gravity, friction, or whatever physically points toward the center.

"},"PHYSC/cheat/c3":{"body":"

📋 Energy & Momentum

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Work & Kinetic Energy

▸ Work W = F·d·cos θ , where F is the force, d the distance moved, and θ the angle between them. Units: joules (1 J = 1 N·m). A force perpendicular to the motion (θ = 90°) does zero work.

▸ Kinetic energy The energy of a moving object: KE = ½mv² . It grows with the square of speed — double the speed, quadruple the energy. Units: joules.

▸ Work-Energy Theorem The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔKE = ½mv² − ½mv₀² . Do positive work and it speeds up; do negative work (like friction) and it slows.

Potential Energy & Conservation

▸ Gravitational PE Energy stored by height: PE = mgh , where h is the height above a reference level. Lift something up and you store this energy; it is released as it falls.

▸ Elastic (spring) PE Energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring: PE = ½kx² , where k is the spring constant and x the displacement from the natural length.

▸ Conservation of energy With no friction, the total mechanical energy is constant: KE + PE = constant . Equivalently, KE₀ + PE₀ = KE_f + PE_f. Energy just shifts between kinetic and potential forms.

Momentum & Impulse

▸ Momentum p = mv — a vector pointing in the direction of motion. Units: kg·m/s. A heavy slow truck and a light fast bullet can have similar momentum.

▸ Impulse J = F·Δt = Δp . A force F acting for time Δt delivers an impulse equal to the change in momentum. Spreading the same momentum change over more time means less force.

Collisions

▸ Momentum conservation For an isolated system, total p before = total p after : m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = m₁v₁′ + m₂v₂′. The internal collision forces are equal and opposite (third law), so they cancel out.

📋 Rotation & Gravitation

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Rotational Kinematics

▸ Rotational kinematics For constant angular acceleration: ω = ω₀ + αt , θ = ω₀t + ½αt² , and ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ — identical in form to the linear equations.

▸ Linear-angular connection A point at radius r from the axis moves with linear speed v = rω and tangential acceleration a = rα . Farther from the axis means faster linear motion for the same rotation.

Torque & Moment of Inertia

▸ Torque τ = r·F·sin θ , where r is the distance from the axis to where the force is applied, F is the force, and θ is the angle between them. Maximum torque comes from pushing perpendicular (θ = 90°), far from the axis. Units: N·m.

▸ Moment of inertia I is rotational mass — resistance to angular acceleration. It depends on both mass and how that mass is distributed : mass farther from the axis gives larger I. For a point mass, I = mr².

▸ Rotational Newton's Second Law τ = Iα — net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration, the rotational twin of F = ma.

Angular Momentum

▸ Angular momentum L = Iω — moment of inertia times angular velocity. Units: kg·m²/s. It is the rotational analog of linear momentum p = mv.

▸ Conservation of angular momentum With no net external torque, L is constant : Iω stays the same. So if I decreases, ω must increase to compensate (and vice versa).

Universal Gravitation

▸ Universal gravitation F = G·m₁·m₂ / r² , where m₁ and m₂ are the masses, r is the distance between their centers, and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² is the gravitational constant. The force is attractive and acts along the line joining them.

▸ Surface gravity The acceleration due to gravity at a distance r from a planet of mass M is g = GM/r² . This is why g ≈ 9.8 m/s² at Earth's surface, and weaker on smaller or less massive worlds.

"},"PHYSC/cheat/c5":{"body":"

📋 Oscillations & Waves

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Simple Harmonic Motion

▸ Simple harmonic motion SHM occurs when the restoring force obeys F = −kx (Hooke's law): the force is proportional to displacement x and points back toward equilibrium (the minus sign). This produces sinusoidal oscillation.

▸ Period of a mass-spring system The time for one full cycle is T = 2π√(m/k) , where m is the mass and k the spring constant. The frequency f = 1/T (cycles per second, in hertz) is how many oscillations occur each second.

Pendulums & Energy in SHM

▸ Pendulum period For small swings, a pendulum of length L has period T = 2π√(L/g) . Remarkably, it does not depend on the mass of the bob or (for small angles) the amplitude — only on length and gravity.

▸ Energy exchange In SHM, total energy is constant but continuously converts: maximum kinetic energy at equilibrium (fastest point) and maximum potential energy at the extremes (turning points, momentarily at rest). KE + PE stays fixed.

Wave Properties

▸ Wave speed v = f·λ — wave speed equals frequency times wavelength. For a fixed medium, v is constant, so higher frequency means shorter wavelength.

▸ Transverse vs longitudinal Transverse: the medium moves perpendicular to the wave's travel (light, waves on a string). Longitudinal: the medium moves parallel to the travel, as compressions (sound).

Sound

▸ Sound waves Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave — air molecules vibrate back and forth along the direction of travel, creating regions of compression and rarefaction. It needs a medium (no sound in a vacuum).

▸ Doppler effect When a sound source moves toward you, the waves bunch up → higher pitch ; moving away, they stretch out → lower pitch . This is why a passing siren drops in pitch as it goes by.

📋 Thermodynamics

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Temperature & Heat

▸ Temperature Temperature reflects the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance. Scales: Celsius (°C), Kelvin (K, where 0 K is absolute zero), and Fahrenheit (°F). Note K = °C + 273.

▸ Heat Heat Q is energy in transit from a hotter object to a cooler one. It is measured in joules. Heat flows until both reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium).

▸ Specific heat The heat needed to change a substance's temperature: Q = mcΔT , where m is mass, c is the specific heat (energy per kg per degree), and ΔT is the temperature change. Water has a famously high c, so it heats and cools slowly.

Laws of Thermodynamics

▸ Zeroth Law If two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other. This is what makes temperature a consistent, measurable quantity.

▸ First Law (energy conservation) ΔU = Q − W : the change in a system's internal energy equals the heat added minus the work it does. Energy is conserved — it only changes form.

▸ Second Law (entropy) The total entropy (disorder) of an isolated system never decreases. Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never the reverse, and no engine can be perfectly efficient.

▸ Third Law As temperature approaches absolute zero (0 K), entropy approaches a minimum. Absolute zero can be approached but never actually reached.

Kinetic Theory & Gas Laws

▸ Ideal gas law PV = nRT , where P is pressure, V is volume, n is the number of moles, R = 8.31 J/(mol·K) is the gas constant, and T is the absolute temperature (in kelvin ). It links all the state variables of a gas.

"},"PHYSC/cheat/c7":{"body":"

📋 Electricity & Magnetism

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Coulomb's Law & Electric Field

▸ Coulomb's law F = k·q₁·q₂ / r² , where q₁ and q₂ are the charges (in coulombs), r is the distance between them, and k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². The force is along the line joining the charges: repulsive for like charges, attractive for opposite.

▸ Electric field The electric field E = F/q is the force per unit charge at a point (units: N/C). A field from a point charge is E = kq/r². Field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative ones.

Electric Potential

▸ Electric potential V = kq/r is the potential (in volts) a distance r from a point charge. The potential energy of a charge q at potential V is U = qV . One volt = one joule per coulomb.

▸ Uniform field relation In a uniform field (like between parallel plates), the potential difference relates to the field by V = E·d , where d is the distance along the field.

Circuits & Ohm's Law

▸ Electric current I = Q/t — charge flowing per unit time, measured in amperes (1 A = 1 C/s).

▸ Ohm's law V = I·R — voltage equals current times resistance (R in ohms , Ω). More voltage drives more current; more resistance reduces it.

▸ Electric power P = I·V (also P = I²R) — the rate energy is delivered, in watts. This is what your electric bill measures.

Magnetism

▸ Force on a moving charge A charge q moving at speed v through a magnetic field B feels a force F = qvB (when v is perpendicular to B). The force is perpendicular to both v and B, and a stationary charge feels no magnetic force.

▸ Force on a current-carrying wire A wire of length L carrying current I in a field B feels a force F = BIL (for perpendicular orientation). This is what makes motors turn.

▸ Right-hand rule Point your right hand's fingers along the velocity (or current), curl toward the field B, and your thumb gives the force direction (for a positive charge). It is the standard way to find the direction of magnetic force.
